title: Motion in a Straight Line — Chapter Summary
intro: This chapter introduces kinematics — the precise vocabulary for describing motion: position, displacement, velocity, acceleration. For the special case of motion in a straight line under constant acceleration, three equations connect everything; we use them on free-fall problems and read motion off graphs.

sections.heading: Position, distance, displacement
bullets: Position is the signed coordinate of an object relative to the origin.
Distance is the total path length (scalar, ≥ 0).
Displacement is the change in position (vector in 1D, signed).
Distance ≥ |displacement|; equality when motion is in one direction.
Both quantities have SI unit metre.

sections.heading: Velocity and speed
bullets: Average velocity = Δx / Δt; average speed = total distance / total time.
Instantaneous velocity v(t) = dx/dt = slope of tangent to the x–t graph.
Average speed and |average velocity| match for unidirectional motion only.
Speed is always positive; velocity can be positive or negative in 1D.
SI unit: m/s.

sections.heading: Acceleration
bullets: Average acceleration = (v − u) / Δt.
Instantaneous acceleration a(t) = dv/dt = slope of v–t graph.
Uniform acceleration: a is constant in magnitude AND direction.
Signs of v and a are independent: an object can have v > 0 with a < 0 (slowing down).
SI unit: m/s².

sections.heading: Kinematic equations
bullets: For constant a: v = u + at; s = ut + (1/2) a t²; v² = u² + 2 a s.
All three are derivable from the definitions.
Apply ONLY when a is constant.
s in the second and third equations is displacement (not distance).
Useful corollary: distance in n-th second S_n = u + a (n − 1/2).

sections.heading: Free fall
bullets: Near Earth's surface, g ≈ 9.8 m/s² downward (often 10 m/s² for estimates).
Take 'up' as +; then a = −g.
Time to apex t_up = u / g; max height h_max = u² / (2 g).
Time of flight back to launch height: t_total = 2 u / g.
Body returns to launch height with the same speed |u|.

sections.heading: Motion graphs
bullets: x–t graph: slope = velocity; horizontal line = at rest; straight sloped = uniform v.
v–t graph: slope = acceleration; horizontal = uniform v; straight sloped = uniform a.
Area under v–t graph = displacement.
v–t graph crossing the time axis ↔ direction of motion reverses.
For uniform a starting from rest, x(t) is a parabola; v(t) is a straight line through origin.

key_takeaways: Distance is scalar; displacement is a signed vector; they only agree for unidirectional motion.
Velocity is the slope of an x–t graph; acceleration is the slope of a v–t graph.
The three kinematic equations apply ONLY for constant acceleration.
Free fall is just constant-acceleration motion with a = g, downward.
The area under a v–t graph is displacement; the slope is acceleration.
An object can be momentarily at rest while still accelerating (e.g. apex of a vertical throw).

The signed coordinate of an object measured from the origin along a chosen direction.
The total length of the path travelled (scalar).
The change in position from start to end (vector in 1D, signed).
Δx / Δt over a time interval; a vector.
The limit of average velocity as Δt → 0; equals dx/dt.
The magnitude of the velocity (always non-negative).
The rate of change of velocity; a = dv/dt.
Acceleration constant in magnitude and direction throughout the motion.
Motion under gravity alone, with constant downward acceleration g and air resistance neglected.
The total time spent in the air for a vertical throw between launch and return to launch height.
The peak height reached by an object thrown vertically; for an initial speed u, h_max = u² / (2g).
A plot of position vs time; its slope at any point is the instantaneous velocity.
A plot of velocity vs time; its slope is the acceleration and the area under it is the displacement.
